If you ask some one who says they are a survivalists or a prepper: "What are the top 5 things that you must have for any kind of long term survival. Here in my opinion at the top 5 in order of importance that you must have

  1. Water. (Water is life. All living things need it and with out it you die)

  2. Shelter. In North America with our varied and extreme climate with out shelter you are going to die of sunstroke or freeze to death. In addition you must have shelter to store what few supplies andd food you have. With out shelter your food is going to go to hell, be eaten by pests, or just generally degrade. You also need shelter to keep your equipment up to operational condition. Knives, axes, shovels, tools will become useless if not protected from the weather. Also if you want to maintain optimal health you must have good shelter. Of course the more substantial shelter you have the better off you will be. A tent just isn't going to do it.

  3. Fuel. Liquid or gaseous Fuel in an emergency is going to become impossible to get. With out fuel you cannot cook your food, or heat your shelter. Fuel is more important that food for the following reason. Lets say you have a cooked piece of food that will yield 500 calories. It will take and expenditure of about 60-100 calories to digest the food leaving 400 to 440 calories for your body to use for other body functions. However is the food is raw then is calorie content will be between 350 to 400 calories. (cooking breaks down some of the non-digestable content of the food to something the body can use. Also raw food take two to three time the energy to digest than cooked food. So now you have 375 calories and it takes 150 calories to digest the food which leaves you with 225 calories for use by your body. This means you are going to have to spend twice as much time foraging for food and twice the amount of time eating and digesting it. So now you must spend all your time sleeping eating and moving and doing nothing else. I think this is the Law of diminishing returns. And then there is the problem with uncooked food being toxic to your system which can and will kill you.

  4. In an emergency food will be the second thing to disappear. When the trucks stop running and the looters get through looting there isn't going to be any food left. You may a supply of food but that will eventually run out. You must have a way you can replenish your food supplies easily and the only way you can do that is by farming. So your food supply will need a good supply of seeds for growing your follow on crops. Also a few pigs, rabbits an chickens will be necessary. Pigs, rabbits and chickens multiply rapidly and grow to slaughter size even faster on food of poor quality. (Table scraps anyone)

  5. Clothing. (This is the thing that every survivalist or prepper bull shit artist misses) Clothing keep you warm in cold weather and protects your skin. If things go to hell you won't be taking a shower every day or maybe every week. The human skin is the home of some very nasty fungus and bacteria. If you get a cut, scrape, or a wound you are going to get an infection. At the least an infection decreases your mobility. At the worst infection will kill you. Also good boots are mandatory. Now here is the $64 question? How long will your clothes last if you can't change them and wash them? How does 30 days grab you. If you ever see refugees one of the things that you will notice is the ragged condition of their clothes. Wearing clothes all the time allows dirt to be packed in between the fibers. I bought a Sprint-based first gen Moto X when they came out and had to wait a year before I could bring it over because Spring has an exclusivity contract with Motorola. In terms of cost, I can't beat it. Since I average 2GB of data, there is no need for me to look for unlimited data plans. Even when I was on Verizon and had unlimited (I was grandfathered in for a few years after they killed that plan off) I never used more than 3GB of data. So, in short, my bill, with 2 phones, averages around 50 bucks a month.
